client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away about two months ago. At work, I just stare at my screen and can't get anything done — my mind keeps drifting, and then I feel guilty for not being productive, which makes everything worse. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying right now — the grief, the difficulty concentrating, the guilt on top of it all — makes complete sense given what you've been through. Losing your father just two months ago is a profound loss, and your mind drifting isn't a failure; it's grief doing what grief does. Even coming here with some doubt about whether it will help takes courage, and that willingness to try something is actually a meaningful first step.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, hearing that my mind drifting "makes sense" doesn't really make me feel better about the pile of unfinished work sitting on my desk. Like, my boss doesn't care that I'm grieving — deadlines still exist, and I'm falling behind, and that just adds another layer of stress on top of everything. I guess I just don't see how talking about it fixes the practical problem of me not being able to function.
therapist: You're absolutely right that talking doesn't make the deadlines disappear, and I don't want to brush past that real pressure you're under. What I'm noticing is that the guilt and grief seem to be feeding each other in a cycle — the grief makes it hard to focus, the unfinished work makes you feel worse, and that weight makes it even harder to function. What if we worked on some concrete strategies to help you manage that cycle, so you can start to get some traction at work even while you're grieving?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, I can see what you mean about the cycle — I hadn't really thought about it that way, but yeah, it does feel like one thing makes the other worse. I'm just not sure what "concrete strategies" would even look like when some days I can barely get myself out of bed, let alone organize my workload. What kind of strategies are you thinking, because if it's something like "make a to-do list," I've tried that and it just becomes another thing I feel bad about not finishing.
therapist: You're so right to push back on that — a to-do list can actually backfire when you're grieving, because it sets up another opportunity to feel like you're failing. What I'm thinking is something smaller and more forgiving, like identifying just one "good enough" task for a day, something so manageable that finishing it actually gives you a tiny sense of traction rather than highlighting everything else undone. Does that feel like something your brain could work with, or does even that feel like too much pressure on the harder days?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean, one task does sound less overwhelming than a whole list, so maybe that's more realistic. But here's what I'm worried about — some days that one task still doesn't get done, and then I'm back to feeling like a failure again, just with a shorter list. I guess I'm not sure how to stop that guilt from kicking in no matter how small I make the goal.
therapist: That guilt response is really the heart of it — it sounds like your brain has learned to treat any incomplete task as evidence of failure, rather than as just an incomplete task. In CBT we'd call that a thinking trap, where the meaning you attach to not finishing something ("I'm a failure") is doing far more damage than the unfinished task itself. What do you think it would look like to separate the task from what it means about you — so that a bad day is just a bad day, not proof of something?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I understand the concept, like intellectually it makes sense that a bad day is just a bad day. But my dad just died, and I feel like I should be pushing through and being stronger, and when I can't even finish one small thing it feels like I'm letting everyone down — including him somehow. I don't know how you just decide to stop a thought from meaning something when it feels so real and so tied up in everything.
therapist: The way you just said that — there's something that sounds almost fragile underneath it, like you're holding something much heavier than even your words are letting on, and I want to gently stay with that for a moment. This idea that you should be "stronger," that somehow not finishing a task is letting your dad down — that's not just a thinking trap, that sounds like grief mixed with love, like you're trying to honor him by being harder on yourself. I'm wondering, what do you think your dad would actually say if he could see you right now, struggling but still trying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: That question actually hit me harder than I expected, because honestly, my dad was never the kind of person who pushed me to be tough — he would have told me to take it easy on myself, that's just who he was. And now I feel kind of stupid for not seeing that I've been doing the opposite of what he would have wanted. But knowing that and actually feeling it are two completely different things, and I don't know how to get from one to the other.
therapist: Please don't feel stupid — what you just did took real insight, and the fact that it landed so hard tells me it actually means something deep to you. That gap between knowing and feeling is one of the most human things there is, and it's especially hard when the person who would have helped you believe it is the one you're grieving. I wonder if, over time, we could start to let his voice become part of how you talk to yourself — not as a rule to follow, but as a kind of gentleness you're slowly learning to borrow from him.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea of borrowing his gentleness — I actually like how you put that, because it doesn't feel like I'm betraying the grief by doing it, if that makes sense. But I'm also a little scared that if I start being softer on myself, I'll just completely fall apart and stop functioning altogether, like the guilt is somehow the only thing holding me together right now. I don't know if that sounds crazy, but it feels true.
therapist: It doesn't sound crazy at all — it actually makes a lot of sense that guilt has started to feel like structure when everything else feels so unsteady, like it's the scaffolding keeping you upright. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if the grief itself is what's holding you together, and the guilt is actually just adding extra weight on top of it? Softening toward yourself doesn't mean the grief disappears or that you stop caring — it might actually let you carry it more honestly, the way your dad would have wanted you to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That reframe actually does something for me — the idea that grief is the thing holding me together, not the guilt, feels more true than I expected it to. I think I've been confusing the two, like I thought if I stopped feeling guilty it meant I didn't care about losing him, but maybe that's not right. I'm still not sure I know how to actually practice that in the moment when the guilt hits, but I feel like I understand something a little differently right now.
therapist: What you just named — that guilt and grief aren't the same thing — is actually a really significant shift, and I don't want to rush past it even though I notice you're already moving toward "but how do I practice it." When the guilt hits in the moment, one small thing you can try is asking yourself: "Is this grief, or is this punishment?" — because grief connects you to him, and punishment just isolates you. That one question might not stop the guilt, but it could help you see it more clearly instead of being swept away by it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question — "is this grief or is this punishment" — actually feels like something I could maybe remember in the moment, which is more than I can say for most things people suggest. I'm a little worried that in the thick of it, when I'm staring at my screen at work and spiraling, I won't have the presence of mind to even think to ask it. But I guess it's worth trying, and it's at least something that connects back to him rather than just feeling like a therapy exercise.
therapist: The fact that it connects back to him rather than feeling like a generic exercise actually matters a lot — meaning is what makes these things stick. And you're right that in the middle of a spiral it's hard to access anything, so it might help to make it even more personal, like imagining his voice asking it rather than just the words themselves. That way it's not just a technique you're trying to remember — it's almost like he's there with you in that moment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually made me tear up a little, which I wasn't expecting, and I'm not sure if that's a good sign or if I'm just getting overwhelmed. I think I'm worried that trying to imagine his voice might make the missing him feel even sharper, like it could make things harder before it makes them easier. But I also think you might be right that it's worth that, because right now he feels really far away and maybe this is a way to keep him a little closer.
therapist: Those tears aren't a sign that something is wrong — they're a sign that something real just happened, and that's actually exactly where healing lives. You named something really beautiful just now: that the sharpness of missing him and the closeness of him aren't opposites, they're the same thing, and letting yourself feel that is not falling apart. I think you've done something important today, and I want you to be gentle with yourself about whatever comes up after this conversation.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
